screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we learn a practical workflow for getting useful requirements from real people and turning those discoveries into clear, actionable documentation. Then we will move to documentation formats that teams commonly use: concise user stories for agile conversations and detailed use cases for step-by-step interactions. Think about a feature you care about — how would you test your assumptions with one quick interview and one small prototype? That question is the thread you will follow through the module.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Focus
screens.narratorSegment: This screen focuses on how to practice and measure the objectives you just saw. Start by running a short structured interview to collect specific examples of current workflows and pain points. Then, run a small observation session with one or two users to compare what people say with what they do. Next, draft three user stories for distinct roles or goals that reflect the patterns you observed. Finally, expand one of those stories into a use case that includes preconditions, a main flow, and at least one alternate flow. The hands-on tasks help you move knowledge into skill: interviews and observation reveal context; stories make requirements communicative; use cases make them testable. Assessments might ask which technique best uncovers hidden workarounds or to convert a story into a use case. Regular short cycles — interview, draft, validate with a prototype — keep requirements reliable and reduce rework. Practice with a real small feature, like a short-video sharing flow, to get immediate feedback and refine your documentation skills.

screens.title: What is Requirements Elicitation?
screens.narratorSegment: Requirements elicitation is the active process of engaging stakeholders to discover their needs, expectations, and constraints. It is not merely asking questions and recording answers; it is a deliberate practice that mixes listening, observation, and validation until requirements are clear enough to guide decisions. Elicitation works because people often cannot state their needs precisely — they describe workarounds, show frustration, or indicate priorities through action. For example, a customer might say they want a faster checkout, but observation of their session may reveal the real issue is slow image loading or a confusing address form. The definition we rely on emphasizes interaction: interviews, workshops, observation, surveys, and prototypes are the tools. A common misconception is that a single interview or a long requirements document is sufficient. In reality, multiple techniques combined produce a more complete picture. The takeaway is practical: choose methods that surface hidden steps, test assumptions with prototypes, and treat elicitation as iterative. Ask open questions, seek concrete examples, and verify interpretations with stakeholders to avoid costly misunderstandings later. What is Requirements Elicitation? means elicitation is an iterative, mixed-method process that turns tacit knowledge into explicit, testable requirements.. In practical terms, understanding the art of drawing requirements from people and context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What is Requirements Elicitation?
Definition

Requirements elicitation is the deliberate practice of engaging stakeholders through interviews, workshops, observation, surveys, and prototyping to uncover needs that guide design and development.

• Elicitation is iterative — expect to revisit requirements.
• Techniques reveal different kinds of information: interviews reveal motives, observation reveals actual steps.
• Validation through prototypes confirms assumptions early.
Concrete Example
A product manager runs a 15-minute interview with a power user who says they need faster reporting. Observing the user shows manual CSV exports and spreadsheets are the true bottleneck. The team prototypes a single click export and validates the improvement before specifying acceptance criteria.
Common mistake
Assuming a verbal requirement is complete without requesting examples or observing the user's environment.
Practical checklist
  • • Prepare open-ended questions and examples to prompt specifics.
  • • Use short prototyping to test assumptions quickly.
  • • Combine interviews with observation when possible.
  • • Record concrete scenarios and acceptance criteria.
Key Takeaway

Treat elicitation as iterative and mixed-method. Use concrete examples and prototypes to validate requirements early.

screens.title: Interviews: Structured and Unstructured
screens.narratorSegment: Interviews are one of the most flexible elicitation techniques and come in two common forms: structured and unstructured. A structured interview uses a predefined set of questions so you can compare responses across multiple stakeholders. This is useful when you want measurable input or when interviewing a group of similar users. An unstructured interview is more conversational and lets users lead the discussion to topics that matter most to them. It often reveals unexpected needs but can be harder to compare across participants. In both cases, the quality of your questions matters: ask open-ended questions that encourage examples, avoid yes-or-no phrasing, and probe when answers are vague. For instance, instead of asking 'Do you like the search feature?' ask 'Walk me through the last time you used search. What worked and what slowed you down?' A common mistake is leading the interviewee toward a solution; keep questions neutral and confirm your understanding with short summaries. As a practice step, prepare three open-ended questions for a 10-minute interview, listen for concrete tasks or workarounds, and follow up with a short prototype or observation to validate what you heard.

keyIdea.title: Interview tip
keyIdea.text: Favor open-ended prompts and ask for concrete examples; avoid leading or solution-focused questions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Interviews
Structured vs Unstructured
• Structured: consistent questions, easier to compare answers across stakeholders.
• Unstructured: conversational, reveals unexpected insights, harder to aggregate.
• Combine both when possible: structured core with time for open discussion.
Good question examples
  • • "Tell me about the last time you completed this task."
  • • "What part of the process causes the most delay?"
  • • "Can you show me an example or explain in detail?"
Practical walkthrough
Prepare 3 open-ended questions, run a 10-minute interview, capture direct quotes and the tasks described, then list possible follow-ups to observe or prototype.
Common mistake
Leading the interviewee toward a specific solution or using loaded terms. Stop and restate what you heard to confirm accuracy.

screens.title: Workshops and JAD Sessions
screens.narratorSegment: Workshops, including Joint Application Development sessions, bring multiple stakeholders together to co-design requirements. They are powerful because they create a shared context: users, business experts, and developers discuss goals, resolve conflicts, and produce artifacts in real time. A successful workshop requires a clear agenda, skilled facilitation, and artifacts to work from — a prototype, scenario, or sample workflow. Workshops accelerate alignment and can surface trade-offs quickly, but they also risk being dominated by a few voices or drifting without focused facilitation. To run an effective session, define objectives, prepare a short framing example, use small group activities to draw quieter participants in, and end with clear, assigned next steps. For example, a half-day workshop on a video-sharing feature might start with user scenarios, sketch a simple flow, and end with prioritized user stories and owners for follow-up. A misconception is that workshops replace other techniques; they are most effective when paired with interviews and observation so the group works from real context rather than assumptions. The practical result should be a set of clarified requirements and a plan to document them as stories or use cases.

keyIdea.title: Workshop benefit
keyIdea.text: Workshops create shared understanding quickly, but need facilitation to prevent dominance and scope creep.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Workshops & JAD
Why run a workshop?
• Builds shared mental models across roles.
• Resolves conflicting priorities in the room.
• Produces rapid, collective decisions and artifacts.
Facilitation checklist
  • • Clear agenda and intended outputs.
  • • Short framing example or prototype.
  • • Breakout activities to include quieter voices.
  • • Defined next steps and owners at the end.
Example session
A workshop for short-video features: opening 10 minutes of user scenarios, 30 minutes of sketching flows in small groups, and 20 minutes to produce prioritized user stories and assignments for follow-up prototypes.
Common mistake
Assuming a workshop replaces interviews or observation. Workshops work best when informed by earlier individual research.

screens.title: Surveys, Questionnaires, and Observation
screens.narratorSegment: Surveys and questionnaires let you gather quantitative or structured feedback from many users quickly. They help you find trends, measure priorities, or validate hypotheses across a population. However, they tend to miss nuanced behaviors and often rely on what people say rather than what they do. Observation complements surveys by showing real behavior in context — how users complete tasks, where they hesitate, and what informal steps they take. For deep workflow understanding, observation is often more revealing than interviews or surveys because users may rely on shadow processes they do not report. A simple approach is to combine methods: use observation or interviews to generate hypotheses, then run a short survey to see how widespread a finding is. For example, if observation finds users repeatedly exporting data to work around a missing report, a survey can estimate how many users do that and how often. A common misconception is that surveys are a substitute for talking to users; instead, treat surveys as a way to measure and prioritize findings uncovered by qualitative methods. Surveys, Questionnaires, and Observation means use observation for depth, surveys for breadth, and combine them to validate real user behaviors at scale.. In practical terms, choosing between broad quantitative input and deep qualitative insight. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Surveys & Observation
Surveys
• Good for measuring trends across many users.
• Use clear, short questions and avoid leading language.
• Best for prioritization after qualitative discovery.
Observation
• Reveals actual steps, workarounds, and context-specific problems.
• Often shows what users do, not what they think they do.
• Short sessions can reveal high-impact usability gaps.
Combined workflow
  1. Observe or interview a small set of users to form hypotheses.
  2. Create survey questions to measure those hypotheses at scale.
  3. Use results to prioritize features and follow-up research.
Practical example
Observation finds manual exports. A short survey asks how often users export data and why. If many users export daily, prioritize a built-in report feature and validate with a prototype.

screens.title: Prototyping to Validate Assumptions
screens.narratorSegment: Prototyping is creating a preliminary version of a feature or interface so stakeholders can see and interact with an idea. Prototypes range from rough paper sketches to clickable mockups. Their value lies in turning talk into tangible behavior: users can react to interactions rather than imagining them. When you prototype, you test assumptions quickly and cheaply and often reveal missing requirements or contradictions. For example, a prototype of a short-video creation flow might show how users record, trim, and publish a clip. Stakeholders may notice missing confirmation or privacy options that did not come up in interviews. A common misconception is that prototypes must be high fidelity; lower-fidelity mocks are often enough to validate the flow and encourage useful feedback. Use prototyping after initial elicitation — interviews or observation supply context — and before writing exhaustive specifications. The expected outcome is clearer acceptance criteria and fewer surprises during development. Make the prototype purpose-driven: test a single hypothesis per prototype and capture specific feedback to update user stories or use cases. Prototyping to Validate Assumptions means validate one assumption per prototype and use the results to refine stories and use cases.. In practical terms, use prototypes to convert abstract needs into concrete feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Prototyping
Purpose of prototypes
• Make abstract requirements concrete and testable.
• Reveal missing acceptance criteria and hidden flows.
• Prioritize learning: low-fidelity is often enough early on.
Practical tip
Prototype one interaction at a time and ask specific questions during validation, for example: "Can you complete this task? What surprised you?"
Concrete example
A clickable mock of the video trim UI reveals users want a clearer undo action. The team updates the user story and the prototype before finalizing acceptance criteria.
Avoid this mistake
Expecting a prototype to capture every use case. Prototypes validate assumptions, not specify every edge case.

screens.title: User Stories: Structure and Purpose
screens.narratorSegment: User stories are brief descriptions of a feature from the perspective of an end user and follow a simple template: 'As a [type of user], I want [some goal] so that [some reason/benefit].' Their purpose is not to be exhaustive specifications but to act as placeholders for a conversation between product, design, and engineering. Stories emphasize user value and keep teams focused on why a feature matters. For example, 'As a registered customer, I want to save items to a wishlist so that I can purchase them later' states actor, goal, and benefit clearly. Common mistakes include making stories too large or detailed — turning them into epics or pseudo-specifications — or writing them in technical language that non-technical stakeholders cannot validate. A good practice is to keep stories small, include acceptance criteria that describe observable behavior, and link to a prototype or example when clarity is needed. Stories are particularly useful in agile environments because they are easy to prioritize, split, and discuss during planning. When in doubt, run a short conversation with a stakeholder to confirm the story's value and scope.

keyIdea.title: Story principle
keyIdea.text: User stories should be concise, role-focused, and designed to start conversations, not replace them.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › User Stories
Format
As a [type of user], I want [some goal] so that [some reason/benefit].
Examples
• As a registered customer, I want to save items to a wishlist so that I can purchase them later.
• As an administrator, I want to reset user passwords so that I can help users regain access to their accounts.
Acceptance criteria
Attach short, testable criteria to each story. Example: 'Given a saved item, when I view my wishlist, then the item appears with an add-to-cart button.'
Pitfall
Do not over-engineer stories into long specifications. If the team needs details, link a use case or prototype instead.

screens.title: Use Cases: Actors, Flows, and Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Use cases are a more detailed way to document how an actor interacts with a system to achieve a goal. They list the actor, the goal, preconditions, postconditions, the main flow, and alternate flows. This structure is valuable when you need to describe sequences of steps, error handling, or variations that matter to design and testing. For example, a use case for 'Log In to System' lists the registered user as the actor, requires an active account as a precondition, and describes the main flow: navigate, display login form, enter credentials, validate, and redirect to dashboard. It then notes an alternate flow for invalid credentials with error messaging and retry. Use cases help teams reason about success and failure paths and define acceptance criteria that cover both. A typical mistake is to document too many UI specifics or every tiny branch; keep the use case focused on meaningful variations that affect behavior. Use cases bridge user stories and technical design: write them when a story's implementation requires clarity about flows or when testing needs explicit alternate scenarios. Use Cases: Actors, Flows, and Exceptions means use cases clarify sequential interactions and exceptions so development and testing align on behavior.. In practical terms, structure a use case so interactions and alternate paths are clear. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. narration.text: Use cases are a more detailed way to document how an actor interacts with a system to achieve a goal. They list the actor, the goal, preconditions, postconditions, the main flow, and alternate flows. This structure is valuable when you need to describe sequences of steps, error handling, or variations that matter to design and testing. For example, a use case for 'Log In to System' lists the registered user as the actor, requires an active account as a precondition, and describes the main flow: navigate, display login form, enter credentials, validate, and redirect to dashboard. It then notes an alternate flow for invalid credentials with error messaging and retry. Use cases help teams reason about success and failure paths and define acceptance criteria that cover both. A typical mistake is to document too many UI specifics or every tiny branch; keep the use case focused on meaningful variations that affect behavior. Use cases bridge user stories and technical design: write them when a story's implementation requires clarity about flows or when testing needs explicit alternate scenarios. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Use Cases
Use case elements
  • • Actor: who initiates the interaction.
  • • Goal: what the actor wants to achieve.
  • • Preconditions/Postconditions: start and end states.
  • • Main Flow and Alternate Flows: success and exception paths.
When to use a use case
When behavior depends on ordered steps, error handling, or multiple actors. Use cases help testers and developers agree on scenarios to implement and verify.
Example: Log In to System
Actor: Registered User
Goal: Gain access to protected features
Preconditions: User has an active account
Main Flow:
  1. User navigates to login page.
  2. System displays login form.
  3. User enters username and password.
  4. User submits form.
  5. System validates credentials and redirects to dashboard.
Alternate Flow (Invalid Credentials):
  1-4 as above
  5. System displays "Invalid username or password" and offers retry.
Avoid
Capturing every UI pixel or every rarely-used branch. Focus on meaningful alternative flows that affect behavior or user value.

screens.title: User Stories vs Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: User stories and use cases serve different purposes and are complementary. A user story is a short, user-focused sentence that expresses value and is meant to start a conversation. A use case is a structured, step-by-step description that lists actors, preconditions, main flows, and alternate flows. Use a user story when you need a lightweight, prioritizable unit of work that teams can estimate and deliver. Use a use case when the interaction involves ordered steps, conditional branches, or error handling that must be described precisely for design or testing. For example, 'save to wishlist' is a story that explains value; if the wishlist process has multiple flows, sharing, or payment interactions, expand the story into a use case to make those flows explicit. A common misconception is that both formats are interchangeable; they are not. Overusing use cases makes documentation heavy and slow to maintain, while over-relying on stories can leave out critical exception handling. The best practice is to keep stories as the default and create use cases selectively when clarity about sequences and exceptions is required. User Stories
• Short, role-focused, invite conversation.
• Easy to prioritize and split for agile delivery.

Use Cases

• Useful for complex interactions and testing.

Decision guide

screens.title: Common Pitfalls in Elicitation and Documentation
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring pitfalls undermine elicitation and documentation. First, leading or loaded questions bias responses and hide true needs. Second, capturing too much UI detail in early requirements turns flexible stories into brittle specifications that block creativity. Third, assuming a single technique suffices — for example, a survey alone — can miss context-specific workarounds. Fourth, failing to validate assumptions with prototypes or observation leads to built artifacts that don’t meet user needs. For example, a team might implement a requested toolbar because it was suggested in an interview, only to discover from observation that the toolbar is rarely used and users prefer keyboard shortcuts. To avoid these mistakes, use neutral, open-ended questions; combine methods; prototype critical assumptions; and keep documentation proportional: stories for negotiation, use cases for complex flows. Also capture acceptance criteria that are testable and run brief validation cycles. The final step is reflection: after each elicitation round, ask what you learned, what surprised you, and what you should validate next. Common Pitfalls in Elicitation and Documentation means avoid leading questions, over-specification, single-method research, and skip validation; iterate and validate instead.. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Common Pitfalls
Leading questions
Avoid questions that suggest a desired answer. Instead, ask for examples of recent tasks and frustrations to learn concrete needs.
Over-specification
Recording too many UI details early makes requirements hard to change. Capture intent and outcomes, not fixed UI arrangements.
Single-method reliance
Relying on surveys or interviews alone misses behavior; triangulate with observation and prototypes.
No validation
Failing to prototype or test assumptions leads to rework. Validate the riskiest assumptions quickly.

screens.title: Practice: Stories and a Use Case for Short Video
screens.narratorSegment: This practical exercise uses a short-video feature as our scenario. First, write three user stories that cover distinct roles or goals. For example: 1) As a content creator, I want to record a short clip so that I can share it with followers. 2) As a viewer, I want to like a clip so that I can show appreciation. 3) As a registered user, I want to save drafts so that I can post later. These concise stories capture value for different roles. Next, choose one story and expand it into a use case. If you pick the recording story, list the actor, goal, preconditions, postconditions, the main flow, and an alternate flow. For instance, preconditions might include camera permission granted; postconditions might include the clip saved to the user's drafts or published. The main flow would include steps like open camera, record clip, trim, add caption, and publish. An alternate flow might cover permission denied or upload failure with retry. The goal is to create documentation that a developer or tester can use to implement and verify the feature. Finally, reflect: which assumptions did you need to validate, and how would you test them quickly with a prototype or observation?

Task 1 — Three user stories
• As a content creator, I want to record a short clip so that I can share it with followers.
• As a viewer, I want to like a clip so that I can show appreciation.
• As a registered user, I want to save drafts so that I can post later.
Task 2 — Expand a use case
Use Case: Record and Save Draft
Actor: Content Creator
Goal: Create and save a short video draft
Preconditions: Camera permission granted; user logged in
Main Flow:
  1. User opens camera in app.
  2. User records clip.
  3. User trims clip and adds caption.
  4. User saves draft.
Postconditions: Draft saved and accessible from drafts list
Alternate Flow (Permission Denied):
  1. System requests permission; if denied, prompt user to enable in settings.
Reflection & next step
Identify one assumption to validate — for example, whether users want to save drafts or prefer immediate publishing — and test it with a one-screen prototype or quick observation session.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we learn a practical workflow for getting useful requirements from real people and turning those discoveries into clear, actionable documentation. You will learn several elicitation techniques — interviews, workshops, surveys, observation, and prototypes — and when each method helps you find different kinds of information. Then we will move to documentation formats that teams commonly use: concise user stories for agile conversations and detailed use cases for step-by-step interactions. Practical examples show how a short user story can be expanded into a use case with preconditions, flows, and alternate paths. We will also call out common pitfalls: asking leading questions, capturing too much UI detail, or treating a user story like a full specification. By the end of the lesson you will be able to choose an elicitation method for a situation, write crisp user stories that prompt conversation, and expand one story into a maintainable use case. Think about a feature you care about — how would you test your assumptions with one quick interview and one small prototype? That question is the thread you will follow through the module.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the right elicitation technique for a situation, write user stories that guide development, and create use cases that describe system interactions in detail. First, you will learn to describe interviews, workshops, observation, surveys, and prototyping and why each uncovers different information from stakeholders. Second, you will practice the user story format so you can capture functional needs as short, testable sentences that invite conversation instead of dictating design. Third, you will expand one story into a use case with actor, preconditions, main flow, and alternate flows so developers and testers share a precise understanding. Finally, you will recognize common pitfalls — for example, asking leading questions, over-specifying UI details, or turning stories into unwieldy requirement documents — and learn practical ways to avoid them. Each objective links to small practice tasks that demonstrate the skill, and each one matters because poor elicitation or unclear documentation creates rework, missed needs, and wasted time. Practice actively: after each technique, try a 10-minute interview or a one-slide prototype to validate your assumptions.

This screen focuses on how to practice and measure the objectives you just saw. Start by running a short structured interview to collect specific examples of current workflows and pain points. Then, run a small observation session with one or two users to compare what people say with what they do. Next, draft three user stories for distinct roles or goals that reflect the patterns you observed. Finally, expand one of those stories into a use case that includes preconditions, a main flow, and at least one alternate flow. The hands-on tasks help you move knowledge into skill: interviews and observation reveal context; stories make requirements communicative; use cases make them testable. Assessments might ask which technique best uncovers hidden workarounds or to convert a story into a use case. Regular short cycles — interview, draft, validate with a prototype — keep requirements reliable and reduce rework. Practice with a real small feature, like a short-video sharing flow, to get immediate feedback and refine your documentation skills.

Requirements elicitation is the active process of engaging stakeholders to discover their needs, expectations, and constraints. It is not merely asking questions and recording answers; it is a deliberate practice that mixes listening, observation, and validation until requirements are clear enough to guide decisions. Elicitation works because people often cannot state their needs precisely — they describe workarounds, show frustration, or indicate priorities through action. For example, a customer might say they want a faster checkout, but observation of their session may reveal the real issue is slow image loading or a confusing address form. The definition we rely on emphasizes interaction: interviews, workshops, observation, surveys, and prototypes are the tools. A common misconception is that a single interview or a long requirements document is sufficient. In reality, multiple techniques combined produce a more complete picture. The takeaway is practical: choose methods that surface hidden steps, test assumptions with prototypes, and treat elicitation as iterative. Ask open questions, seek concrete examples, and verify interpretations with stakeholders to avoid costly misunderstandings later. What is Requirements Elicitation? means elicitation is an iterative, mixed-method process that turns tacit knowledge into explicit, testable requirements.. In practical terms, understanding the art of drawing requirements from people and context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Interviews are one of the most flexible elicitation techniques and come in two common forms: structured and unstructured. A structured interview uses a predefined set of questions so you can compare responses across multiple stakeholders. This is useful when you want measurable input or when interviewing a group of similar users. An unstructured interview is more conversational and lets users lead the discussion to topics that matter most to them. It often reveals unexpected needs but can be harder to compare across participants. In both cases, the quality of your questions matters: ask open-ended questions that encourage examples, avoid yes-or-no phrasing, and probe when answers are vague. For instance, instead of asking 'Do you like the search feature?' ask 'Walk me through the last time you used search. What worked and what slowed you down?' A common mistake is leading the interviewee toward a solution; keep questions neutral and confirm your understanding with short summaries. As a practice step, prepare three open-ended questions for a 10-minute interview, listen for concrete tasks or workarounds, and follow up with a short prototype or observation to validate what you heard.

Workshops, including Joint Application Development sessions, bring multiple stakeholders together to co-design requirements. They are powerful because they create a shared context: users, business experts, and developers discuss goals, resolve conflicts, and produce artifacts in real time. A successful workshop requires a clear agenda, skilled facilitation, and artifacts to work from — a prototype, scenario, or sample workflow. Workshops accelerate alignment and can surface trade-offs quickly, but they also risk being dominated by a few voices or drifting without focused facilitation. To run an effective session, define objectives, prepare a short framing example, use small group activities to draw quieter participants in, and end with clear, assigned next steps. For example, a half-day workshop on a video-sharing feature might start with user scenarios, sketch a simple flow, and end with prioritized user stories and owners for follow-up. A misconception is that workshops replace other techniques; they are most effective when paired with interviews and observation so the group works from real context rather than assumptions. The practical result should be a set of clarified requirements and a plan to document them as stories or use cases.

Surveys and questionnaires let you gather quantitative or structured feedback from many users quickly. They help you find trends, measure priorities, or validate hypotheses across a population. However, they tend to miss nuanced behaviors and often rely on what people say rather than what they do. Observation complements surveys by showing real behavior in context — how users complete tasks, where they hesitate, and what informal steps they take. For deep workflow understanding, observation is often more revealing than interviews or surveys because users may rely on shadow processes they do not report. For example, if observation finds users repeatedly exporting data to work around a missing report, a survey can estimate how many users do that and how often. This practical exercise uses a short-video feature as our scenario. First, write three user stories that cover distinct roles or goals. For example: 1) As a content creator, I want to record a short clip so that I can share it with followers. 2) As a viewer, I want to like a clip so that I can show appreciation. 3) As a registered user, I want to save drafts so that I can post later. These concise stories capture value for different roles. Next, choose one story and expand it into a use case. If you pick the recording story, list the actor, goal, preconditions, postconditions, the main flow, and an alternate flow. For instance, preconditions might include camera permission granted; postconditions might include the clip saved to the user's drafts or published. The main flow would include steps like open camera, record clip, trim, add caption, and publish. An alternate flow might cover permission denied or upload failure with retry. The goal is to create documentation that a developer or tester can use to implement and verify the feature. Finally, reflect: which assumptions did you need to validate, and how would you test them quickly with a prototype or observation?

Let's summarize the most important ideas you should carry forward. First, requirements elicitation is an interactive, iterative practice that includes interviews, workshops, surveys, observation, and prototyping. Each method reveals different information — interviews reveal motives, observation reveals behavior, and surveys provide breadth. Second, user stories are short, role-focused statements that capture value and invite conversation, not exhaustive specifications. Third, use cases are structured descriptions with actor, preconditions, main flow, and alternate flows; they are useful when ordered steps and error handling must be explicit. Remember that these tools are complementary: use stories to prioritize and create a backlog, and expand to use cases selectively when clarity about sequences and exceptions is required. A final reminder: always validate assumptions with prototypes or observation where possible. These checks save time and reduce rework during development. Which method will you reach for first the next time a stakeholder asks for a new feature?

A few practical habits make elicitation and documentation reliable. First, always ask for concrete examples during interviews; details reveal edge cases. Second, combine techniques: follow interviews with brief observation or a prototype to validate what you heard. Third, keep documentation proportional: use user stories for lightweight backlog items and create use cases only when flows or exceptions must be explicit. Fourth, use acceptance criteria so stories are testable. For assessment, ask learners to choose the best elicitation technique for a scenario or convert a story into a use case, as in the sample questions. These habits reduce ambiguity and focus teams on delivering user value. Before you finish, pick one habit to adopt in your next meeting: will you ask for an example, run a 10-minute observation, or prototype the riskiest assumption? That single change will improve the clarity of your requirements.
